status_definitions.supported: Evidence supports the stated direction, sign, and reasoning within the declared scope.
status_definitions.partially_supported: Evidence supports only part of the claim, a narrower population or outcome, or an association rather than the full causal claim.
status_definitions.contradicted: Relevant evidence opposes the claimed direction or sign within the declared scope.
status_definitions.mixed_evidence: Relevant evidence both supports and opposes the same defined claim.
status_definitions.insufficient_evidence: Available evidence does not establish or refute the causal claim.
status_definitions.not_assessable: Undefined variable coding or endpoint makes the proposed direction or sign uninterpretable.

methodology.scope: 2010_45 yo.py, 61 edges, using 25 supplied PDFs (24 unique PDF documents) and 17 saved HTML article records. Two HTML records reproduce existing PDF studies: 39 unique documents total. Direction, sign, and written reasoning were reviewed; numeric strength was excluded.
methodology.age_scope: Adult evidence was required for adult claims. Young-adult and general-adult evidence was treated as partial when it did not report an age-45 or midlife estimate. Pediatric findings were not transferred as adult causal proof.
methodology.causal_standard: Associations, reviews, and clinical recommendations were not automatically treated as proof of causal direction. Undefined categorical signs were marked not_assessable.
methodology.source_limits: This is a validation against the supplied corpus, not a systematic review of all 2010 ADHD literature. A status of insufficient_evidence is not evidence that an edge is false.
methodology.strength: The graph's numeric edge strengths were not validated.
methodology.duplicate: s12402-010-0036-9 (1).pdf is byte-identical to s12402-010-0036-9.pdf. The sex/age PubMed record (PMID 20410711) and ClinicalKey caudate article reproduce AGE_SEX and CAUDATE_MRI PDFs, respectively. Alternate formats are not independent studies.
methodology.html_scope: 15 PubMed records and two publisher records were parsed. Only primary article abstracts are used as new evidence; navigation, related articles and saved asset frames are excluded. ClinicalKey also contains the caudate full text, already supplied as PDF. Bipolar publication year is 2010 from the article date and journal citation, despite conflicting website citation metadata. Abstract encoding artifacts are preserved.
methodology.evidence_limits: Cross-sectional associations, selected prison/Tourette populations, clinical disparity commentary, and QOL endpoints are distinguished from causal exposure effects. QOL treatment gains do not validate diagnosis-only benefits or adverse-effect-only harm. Pediatric findings are not transferred to adult age-specific claims.

edges.existing_reasoning: Genetic vulnerability contributes strongly to lifelong ADHD.
edges.observation_from_validation: Adult and genetic reviews describe ADHD as highly heritable and persistent from childhood, supporting broad lifelong liability more than any specific variant mechanism.
edges.recommended_action: Retain the positive edge, define Genetic Risk as aggregate inherited liability, and avoid implying a known single variant.

evidence.exact_excerpt: Although twin and family studies have shown attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) to be highly heritable, genetic variants influencing the trait at a genome-wide significant level have yet to be identified.
evidence.location: PDF page 1
evidence.relevance: Supports inherited liability while cautioning that individual genome-wide significant variants were not identified.

evidence.exact_excerpt: Adult individuals with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) have been suffering from this neurobiological and highly heritable disorder chronically since childhood.
evidence.location: PDF page 1
evidence.relevance: Supports persistence into adulthood and inherited liability, but does not provide an age-32-specific estimate.

edges.existing_reasoning: Underlying ADHD strongly affects executive functioning.
edges.observation_from_validation: The adult review describes longstanding attentional, emotional-regulation, and disinhibition impairments, consistent with executive dysfunction, but does not identify ADHD as a separate causal exposure. The new adult ERP review adds cognitive-processing context without isolating the practical functional consequences of executive deficits at midlife.
edges.recommended_action: Define the executive-function construct and distinguish diagnostic symptoms from downstream deficits.

evidence.exact_excerpt: Resulting from their longstanding neuropsychological impairments, such as attentional problems, emotional instability, and disinhibition, they are familiar to a multiplicity of negative life outcomes and under-achievement.
evidence.location: PDF page 1
evidence.relevance: Supports a relationship between longstanding impairment and adverse adult outcomes without isolating a single causal edge.

evidence.exact_excerpt: Considering that all three core symptoms of the disorder have a significant impact on both information processing and on concomitant cognitive functions, patients with ADHD should be divided into subgroups based on their neuropsychologically measured dominant symptoms.
evidence.location: [Event-related potentials associated with error detection in adult ADHD--literature review] - PubMed.html; article abstract (#eng-abstract)
evidence.relevance: Adult electrophysiological review: cognitive processing mechanisms, not a controlled executive-deficit-to-practical-impairment effect.

edges.existing_reasoning: ADHD commonly co-occurs with anxiety, mood, or other conditions.
edges.observation_from_validation: New adult bipolar and prison studies document comorbidity and symptom overlap in selected samples. This strengthens adult co-occurrence evidence, but does not show ADHD causing those conditions or supply an exact-age estimate.
edges.recommended_action: Retain as an association with named comorbidities; distinguish screening results and selected populations from causal mechanisms.

evidence.exact_excerpt: Furthermore, a large part of this population suffers from psychiatric comorbidity.
evidence.location: PDF page 1
evidence.relevance: Supports adult co-occurrence, not ADHD causing each comorbid condition.

evidence.exact_excerpt: Conclusions: Our findings illustrate the close relationship between some symptoms of BSD and ADHD in adults.

evidence.relevance: Cross-sectional adult symptom overlap; screening positive is not identical to confirmed bipolar disorder. Clinical assessment ambiguity is supported but actual diagnostic error rates and causation are unmeasured.

evidence.exact_excerpt: The authors conclude that ADHD is common in offenders and is associated with comorbid disorders, worse quality of life, and higher risk for suicidal behaviors.

evidence.relevance: Selected incarcerated adult sample; not representative of all adults. Association of ADHD with QOL does not isolate functional impairment as a cause or diagnosis as a benefit.
